transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-28
Time: 15:00 PT
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Blake, Priya Nair, Marcus Li (Redwood); Sara Chen, Diego Alvarez, Maya Kapoor, Tom Reynolds (Voyager)

Auto-summaries (auto-gen, may be imperfect):
- Summary: prefix cache deep-dive, talk about hit rates, tenant isolation, and next steps to benchmark.
- Action items: run benchmarks, share traffic samples, security follow-up.

[00:00] Jordan Blake: hey everyone, thanks for hopping on. quick intros?
[00:05] Sara Chen: yeah Sara here, infra lead at Voyager. we'll mostly be focused on latency and multi-tenant safety today.
[00:10] Jordan Blake: awesome. priya from our runtime team will lead the technical bits. priya?
[00:15] Priya Nair: hey all. high level — prefix/prompt caching is where we cache model key/value state for common prefixes so you can skip the full attention recompute for the prefix. big win for lat-sensitive flows.
[00:28] Diego Alvarez: quick q — how do you define the prefix? token-based? raw string? we have truncated prompts, templates, and user-specific context.
[00:36] Priya Nair: good q. we usually build keys from the tokenized prefix plus model id + model version + relevant config (e.g., temperature, system messages). tokenization alignment is important — if your tokenizer version differs you'll miss hits.
[00:50] Tom Reynolds: do you ever see false misses because of tiny punctuation diffs? like trailing spaces?
[00:55] Priya Nair: yes. we recommend normalizing canonicalization: trim, normalize whitespace, canonicalize system messages. sometimes we create a hashing layer over the token ids to keep keys compact.
[01:10] Marcus Li: another practical point — consider hierarchical keys: tenant_id|model_id|prefix_hash. that keeps multi-tenant separation explicit.
[01:20] Maya Kapoor: regarding multi-tenant safety — our security folks want guarantees that cached prefixes from one tenant can't be served to another, and that cache can't leak PII. what's the mitigation?
[01:30] Priya Nair: we support tenant-scoped namespaces. caches are keyed by tenant_id by default in Dedicated/private deployments. for hosted, we isolate via namespaces and can optionally encrypt entries at rest using customer KMS in Private mode.
[01:45] Sara Chen: encryption at rest is good. do you have audit logs when cache entries are served? we need to demonstrate who served what and when.
[01:52] Jordan Blake: yes — Redwood Console collects per-request traces with token-level breakdowns, and we can surface cache hit/miss metrics and access logs. those logs can be forwarded to your SIEM.
[02:02] Diego Alvarez: let's talk hit rate expectations. we run a lot of templated prompts (~70% of calls share the same 60-80 token system + user template). what hit rates should we expect?
[02:12] Priya Nair: realistically, if you canonicalize and your prefixes align with tokens, you can see 50-80% hit rates for templated flows. for more variable user content it'll be lower. key factors: prefix granularity and how often you truncate the user payload before the model call.
[02:28] Tom Reynolds: we've also got a feature where we append short user history (last 2 messages) — does that degrade hits?
[02:34] Priya Nair: yes because that increases prefix variance. one pattern: cache only the system message + template prefix and reattach recent user history post-KV fetch. that's a tradeoff — saves compute on early layers but may require more tokens to be processed for the variable tail.
[02:50] Marcus Li: on the runtime side, we also do partial KV reuse — you can fetch the KV for the static prefix and then feed remaining tokens to continue generation; this keeps memory low while preserving hit value.
[03:05] Sara Chen: eviction policy question — LRU vs size-based vs cost-based? we have spikes in traffic and don't want thrashing.
[03:12] Priya Nair: we typically recommend hybrid: tenant-scoped LRU with weighted eviction by token-length and access frequency. for multi-tenant Dedicated pools you can reserve a min quota per tenant to avoid noisy neighbors.
[03:26] Diego Alvarez: and sharding — do you shard the cache across GPUs or nodes? we run on prem with ~8 nodes.
[03:32] Priya Nair: yes, caches are sharded — shard key often = tenant_id mod N or prefix_hash mod N. sharding reduces memory pressure per node but you need consistent routing (sticky routing) so followups hit the same shard. there is also an option for global redis-backed prefix index + local per-node KV for hot items.
[03:50] Maya Kapoor: if we do VPC/private deployment, do you still do sharding the same way? what about network egress between shards inside a VPC?
[03:58] Marcus Li: inside a VPC it's all internal traffic; we can colocate shards with model workers to minimize cross-node transfer. for on-prem air-gapped, we can deploy a single-node cache or configure explicit shard maps.
[04:12] Tom Reynolds: how does batching interact? we need to preserve low p95 latency for interactive sessions but also want throughput for bulk APIs.
[04:20] Priya Nair: batching helps throughput but hurts tail latency. the runtime supports adaptive batching: short timeout for interactive routes and longer for background. cache hits can bypass batching by returning early if the cached KV covers the whole prefix and the request doesn't need re-batching. practically though, some batching windows may still apply for the tail tokens.
[04:40] Sara Chen: quantization — does using int8 or int4 change cache behavior? e.g., you cache KV computed from quantized model — does that cache become incompatible across quantization schemes?
[04:48] Priya Nair: yes — KV is tied to runtime representation. cache keys must include model binary fingerprint and quantization profile. int8 vs int4 differences can lead to different KV formats. Redwood Runtime marks cache entries with model-version + quantization signature to prevent mismatch.
[05:02] Diego Alvarez: do quantized KVs lose fidelity causing downstream hallucinations?
[05:06] Priya Nair: there is some quality delta for aggressive quantization on small models; for large decoder-only models we see minimal impact at int8 with our kernels. we recommend validating on your eval sets. that's one reason to run the benchmark — quality + perf delta.
[05:22] Jordan Blake: we have a benchmark sheet — link (drive.re/redwood-prefix-bench) with sample results for templated workflows. we'll share and add a Voyager-specific run.
[05:32] Tom Reynolds: cache consistency: if we roll out a prompt template change, how do we invalidate old entries?
[05:38] Marcus Li: you can namespace the key with a template version id and perform bulk invalidation by bumping version. we support TTLs and manual invalidation APIs as well. Be careful with negative cache side effects.
[05:52] Maya Kapoor: is there risk of stale cached context being used that contains PII we want to purge (GDPR right to be forgotten)?
[05:58] Priya Nair: for Private deployments you can configure purge APIs and shorter TTLs for sensitive tenants. for Hosted, we also have retention controls and can evict by tenant + key pattern; we can also integrate with your data governance workflows.
[06:12] Diego Alvarez: throughput numbers: what's the per-GPU KV cache capacity and typical memory used?
[06:18] Marcus Li: depends on model and sequence length. rule of thumb: each token's KV projection ~ a few hundred bytes depending on head count and d_k. e.g., a 32k-context model with 2048-dim per head uses more. for common mid-size models, a node can hold tens of thousands of prefixes; we give sizing guidance in the deployment doc.
[06:36] Priya Nair: we'll need your model sizes and avg prefix lengths — that plus top-K prefixes frequency will let us estimate memory. that's why we asked for the top 50 prefixes trace.
[06:48] Sara Chen: latency: if cache hit vs miss delta — what are p50/p95 numbers?
[06:54] Priya Nair: cache hit can shave off 20-200ms depending on model and tokenizer overhead — for smaller models it's modest, for 70B-class models you can see bigger savings. p95 depends on your batching and network hops. we'll include sample p50/p95 in the benchmark.
[07:12] Tom Reynolds: any gotchas with model rollouts and cache invalidation during canarying?
[07:18] Marcus Li: yes, if you route some traffic to new model variant, cache keys must include model variant id; otherwise new requests may pull old KV incompatible with new model. best practice: warm-only traffic to new model and seed its cache as part of rollout.
[07:34] Diego Alvarez: operational costs — is prefix caching always cost-saving?
[07:38] Priya Nair: typically yes for templated heavy workloads, but caching increases memory footprint and needs operational ops for eviction. if your workload is highly unique per request, the hit rate might be low and costs could rise. the Optimize toolkit can recommend which prefixes to cache.
[07:58] Jordan Blake: let's capture the runbook: 1) Voyager share traces; 2) Redwood runs 3 configs; 3) review results & security.
[08:06] Maya Kapoor: one final security note: we need SAML SSO + audit trail for admin actions (cache invalidation). can you support that?
[08:12] Jordan Blake: yes — Redwood Private supports SAML/SSO, RBAC, audit logs, and KMS integrations. we'll add the security whitepaper to the next email.
[08:20] [crosstalk] Diego Alvarez: OK sounds good, thanks.
